title: Reef Fishes Persist Despite Multiple Coral Bleaching Events
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

We assess whether mass coral bleaching events coincide with declines in reef fish communities (abundance and species richness) and whether responses vary with the degree of association with live coral.

Location

Indo-Pacific coral reefs: 933 sites across eight ecoregions.

Time

2009–2024.

Major Taxa Studied

780 reef fish species.

Methods

Using a global fish survey database (Reef life Survey), we document changes in fish abundance and species richness across coral reefs between 2009 and 2024. Species were grouped by their degree of coral association (strong, moderate, non-associated), and trends were compared against documented mass coral bleaching events. Bayesian hierarchical models were used to estimate regional trajectories and associated uncertainties.

Results

Changes in fish communities were highly variable and largely decoupled from mass coral bleaching events. These patterns persisted across the eight ecoregions and were similar irrespective of the strength of fish-coral associations. Contrary to expectations, strongly coral-associated fishes did not record consistent declines in either abundance or richness during bleaching years. Under bleaching regimes, the probability of observing increases or decreases in fish abundance or richness was relatively even. When examining the Great Barrier Reef specifically, neither the severity of bleaching nor the onset of regular bleaching events (≥ 2016) produced marked changes in fish abundance or richness.

Main Conclusions

Our results suggest that even the most coral-dependent fishes have limited, and often unexpected responses to mass coral bleaching events. Reef fish dynamics are strongly context-dependent and are shaped by the interaction of multiple ecological and biophysical processes. Understanding fish community responses to global change requires broad-scale, integrative approaches that move beyond coral-focused perspectives.
